Apple has long positioned privacy as a selling point of its hardware and services, but I sometimes wonder whether Apple now regrets introducing one privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT).

It is a fairly narrow feature, and yet it sometimes feels as if every couple of months there is a new antitrust lawsuit or regulatory challenge to it. A third ATT lawsuit has now been filed in the UK — and this one is a little different.

Apple's response has been added at the end of this article…

The personalised ads controversy

Personalised advertising has been a hot topic of controversy in the tech world for years. Rather than seeing random ads for products we may or may not be interested in, we are shown ads based on our interests — drawn from data collected from the apps we use and the websites we visit.

In theory, this is good for everyone. Consumers see ads they are actually likely to be interested in; advertisers get better returns from precise targeting; and ad-funded apps and websites earn more for the same reason.

Although the data used for personalised advertising is collected anonymously, many people still see the practice as an invasion of privacy. Even though Apple developed a specific technology to ensure the data is anonymous, many consumers remain uneasy about it.

App Tracking Transparency

Apple's App Tracking Transparency was designed to address this concern, giving consumers the choice of whether or not they are happy for their data to be used to serve personalised ads. Developers wanting to collect this data have to ask for consent first.

Unfortunately for the iPhone maker, the measure has drawn a string of lawsuits and antitrust investigations, the main argument being that Apple's own apps don't need to ask for that consent. Apple has repeatedly pointed out that its rules are actually consistent: its own apps don't show the ATT prompt because they don't collect the data ATT covers. Third-party apps that don't collect this data are likewise exempted and don't show the prompt either.

The latest UK lawsuit

Apple has now faced three complaints at the UK's Competition Appeal Tribunal. It lost the first one (though it is currently appealing) and the second is still ongoing.

Reuters has reported on a third lawsuit, filed today.

What's new

There is an interesting twist to the latest lawsuit: it has been brought by Ann Pope, who was herself a senior official at the regulator behind this case.

Ann Pope, a former senior official at the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, is leading the lawsuit. She says Apple's policies "have caused very significant harm to businesses that depend on Apple as a gatekeeper." In a statement, Pope said: "This action is important to protect the rights of UK businesses that depend on Apple, to ensure the rules Apple applies are fair, and to compensate UK companies for the losses they have suffered."

Apple recently agreed to make eight changes to its ATT rules in the EU, following an investigation by Germany's antitrust regulator. Regarding today's lawsuit, Apple has responded to us as follows:

Over the years, numerous privacy advocates have publicly voiced their support for ATT.
